content: Digitalis purpurea, commonly known as Common Foxglove, Purple Foxglove, or Lady's Glove, is a flowering plant belonging to the family Plantaginaceae, though it was previously classified under Scrophulariaceae. It is native to most parts of Europe and is a herbaceous biennial plant. The leaves of Digitalis purpurea are arranged in a spiral pattern, simple in structure, and measure between 10 to 35 cm in length and 5 to 12 cm in width. They are gray-green in color, downy in texture, and have finely toothed margins. During the first year of growth, the leaves form a dense rosette at ground level. In the second year, the plant develops a flowering stem that can grow to a height of 1 to 2 meters. The flowers are arranged in a prominent, terminal, elongated cluster. Each flower is tubular, pendulous, and typically purple, though some cultivars may produce flowers in pink, rose, yellow, or white. The interior of the tubular flowers is often spotted. The plant produces small seeds, approximately 2 mm in size. There are three recognized subspecies of Digitalis purpurea: Digitalis purpurea subsp. purpurea, found across most of Europe. Digitalis purpurea subsp. heywoodii, native to the Iberian Peninsula. Digitalis purpurea subsp. mariana, also native to the Iberian Peninsula. Toxicity Digitalis purpurea contains the cardiac glycoside digitoxin, which renders its leaves, flowers, and seeds toxic to humans and certain animals. Ingestion of any part of the plant can be fatal. The compound digitoxin, extracted from the leaves, was first clinically utilized as a medication for heart failure by William Withering, who observed its ability to reduce dropsy (edema), increase urine output, and exert a significant effect on the heart. Unlike purified pharmacological forms, plant extracts of Digitalis purpurea rarely caused severe intoxication historically because they induced nausea and vomiting shortly after ingestion, preventing further consumption. The primary toxic compounds in Digitalis are the cardiac glycosides digitoxin and digoxin. These compounds exert their effects by inhibiting the ATPase activity of the sodium-potassium ATPase pump (Na+/K+-ATPase), a transmembrane protein complex. This inhibition leads to an increase in intracellular sodium levels, which subsequently raises intracellular calcium levels. The elevated calcium enhances the force of myocardial muscle contractions. At precise dosages, Digitalis toxins can strengthen the heart's contractions. However, the therapeutic window is narrow, meaning even minute increases in dosage can shift the effect from therapeutic to toxic. Symptoms of Digitalis poisoning include a slow pulse rate, nausea, vomiting, and uncoordinated contractions of the heart, which can progress to cardiac arrest and death. Uses Digitalis purpurea is sometimes cultivated in gardens. Under suitable conditions, it self-seeds in areas with partial shade and may become a minor weed. Selected forms of the plant, bred for specific flower colors or dwarf growth habits, are sold as potted plants. Use in Molecular Biology: Digoxigenin Digoxigenin (DIG) is a steroid compound found exclusively in the flowers and leaves of Digitalis purpurea and Digitalis lanata. It is widely used as a molecular probe for detecting DNA or RNA. DIG can be chemically attached to nucleotides, and DIG-labeled uridine (DIG-U) can be incorporated into RNA probes through in vitro transcription. During in situ hybridization, RNA probes containing DIG-U can be detected using anti-DIG antibodies conjugated to alkaline phosphatase. The hybridized transcripts can then be visualized by reacting alkaline phosphatase with a chromogen, producing a colored precipitate.
